title: Technical deep dive: Llama / Mistral / Qwen tuning, MoE routing costs & RoPE scaling
summary: Deep technical session on model-specific inference tuning across Llama, Mistral, and Qwen variants. Covered KV cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs (gptq/bitsandbytes/Q4), MoE routing cost implications, and RoPE scaling/extrapolation. Discussed on-prem/VPC constraints and next steps: run targeted latency benchmarks, hand off benchmark spreadsheet, and scope a short on-prem pilot.
topics: KV cache semantics and cache warming
MoE routing cost and policy (TopK vs noisy gating)
RoPE scaling and sequence length extrapolation
VPC/on-prem install considerations and KMS integration

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE), Sofia Li (Redwood SE), Marcus Nguyen (Redwood Infra), Priya Kapoor (HelixAI ML), Tomás Alvarez (Helix Platform), Lena Schmidt (CTO)

Summary (auto):
- Walkthrough of runtime optimizations per model family (Llama, Mistral, Qwen).
- Deep dive on MoE routing overhead and options to mitigate routing cost.
- RoPE (rotary) scaling: behavior when extrapolating beyond training context length and best practices.
- Operational considerations for Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem) and KMS integration.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jamie Park: alright thanks everyone for joining, this is Jamie from Redwood, we wanted to do a focused session on model-specific tuning 
- Llama, Mistral, Qwen - and then dig into MoE routing cost and RoPE scaling. Sofia's going to lead the perf stuff, Marcus will chime on infra and dedicated/private ops.
[00:18] Priya Kapoor: hey thanks, appreciate it. our main thing is low tail latency for chat workloads, we have a 200ms p50 target and want to understand cost if we go Dedicated or Private. also curious how a MoE model would behave for our routing heavy flows.
[00:32] Sofia Li: great, quick agenda: latency/throughput tradeoffs; KV cache semantics 
- e.g. prefix reuse and cache warming; batching strategies (static vs continuous); quantization effects per model family; then MoE routing, and RoPE scaling. we'll leave 15 min for ops questions.
[00:50] Tomás Alvarez: sounds good. on infra we run on-prem k8s with private network, want to confirm KMS/HSM integration and audit logs, SOC 2 stuff.
[01:05] Marcus Nguyen: yep, Redwood Private supports customer KMS and we can plumb HSM or cloud KMS, audit logs shipped to your SIEM. there's some network reqs for the control plane but data plane can be airgapped if needed.
[01:20] Lena Schmidt: just a note - sequence length for some customers may need 32k tokens in the future, so RoPE scaling/extrapolation is a big one for us.
[01:35] Sofia Li: perfect lead in - i'll start with Llama family. (laughter) so for Llama 2/3, the big wins are 1) optimized kv cache layout - contiguous per-layer KV vs interleaved storage - that affects cache copy costs when you do multi-sequence requests, 2) kernel selection for flash attention variants, and 3) quantization knobs.
[01:58] Priya Kapoor: quick question - for kv cache are we talking about per-request in-memory caches or shared across sessions? we have multi-tenant inference so isolation matters.
[02:12] Sofia Li: good call - we model KV cache as request-scoped by default for privacy, but for pinned sessions (same user) you can enable persistent prefix cache with tenant isolation. persistent cache reduces repeated compute for system prompts and long histories. note: enabling persistent cache increases memory footprint and eviction policy complexity.
[02:35] Tomás Alvarez: when you say eviction, is that LRU or TTL? what's Redwood's default?
[02:44] Marcus Nguyen: default is LRU with configurable TTL per model slot. for Dedicated we let you set memory caps and eviction thresholds; for Private we give the same controls via config map.
[02:55] Sofia Li: moving on batching - continuous batching gives better tokens/sec for high qps, but it raises p95/p99 under bursty traffic. for chat, we usually recommend a hybrid: small batching window (5-15ms) plus async draining for tail requests. we ran experiments on Mistral 7B and saw 2.3x throughput improvement with minimal p95 impact at 10ms window.
[03:25] Priya Kapoor: do those numbers hold for Qwen and larger models?
[03:30] Sofia Li: Qwen tends to have heavier attention compute per token, so throughput uplifts are still there but lower - maybe 1.6x. for 70B Llama, batching strategy must be coupled with kv cache locality - if you batch across different prefixes you'll lose cache benefits. there's a balance: group by prefix-hash to preserve reuse.
[03:50] Tomás Alvarez: grouping by prefix-hash - does Redwood runtime support that natively?
[03:55] Sofia Li: yes, in the router we can partition per-route with a hash key (customer session id or conversation id), and batching respects that key by default for cache-friendly grouping. you can opt out for latency-critical single-shot requests.
[04:10] Jamie Park: quick interjection - anyone here tried MoE on production yet?
[04:15] Priya Kapoor: no, we prototyped a MoE 1B gating layer but saw high variance in latencies. routing overhead looked significant.
[04:22] Sofia Li: that matches our experience - MoE gives parameter/compute savings but routing cost (top-k selection, gating softmax, and sparse attention scatter/gather) adds scheduling and memory overhead. there are two levers: use static routing top-k small (e.g., k=1) to minimize overhead, or batch routing decisions separately. both have tradeoffs for quality.
[04:45] Marcus Nguyen: also the stride on memory access becomes less predictable; on GPUs MoE kernels often require custom scatter-gather kernels. if you're on Dedicated metal with NVLink fabric, routing costs amortize better because of faster inter-GPU comms. on VPC or smaller cluster, you may see >2x p99 compared to dense equivalent.
[05:05] Priya Kapoor: interesting - so for our on-prem with limited NVLink, MoE might be worse for tail latency even if average cost looks better.
[05:12] Sofia Li: exactly. another note: routing cache - we experimented with caching gate decisions for short prefixes, but it can create gating staleness and small quality regressions for dynamic inputs. we usually recommend MoE for throughput-first batch workloads, not low-latency chat.
[05:30] Tomás Alvarez: about quantization - what are the recommended paths? GPTQ? bitsandbytes 4/8?
[05:36] Sofia Li: summary: gptq gives strong 4-bit results for many Llama variants with careful per-channel quantization and some MSE-aware compensation. bitsandbytes 8-bit (LLM.int8) is easiest to integrate but bigger memory. Qwen family is less explored in open-source GPTQ recipes so expect more tuning. for production we run validation evals on held out prompts, and flag hallucination or tokenization drift.
[06:00] Priya Kapoor: any red flags around Q4 and hallucinations or logits shift?
[06:05] Sofia Li: yes, Q4 can cause logit scale drift - we calibrate scales per-layer and retrain a tiny calibration head for some models. Redwood Optimize has a quality monitoring job that checks prompt sets and alerts on perplexity or rerank drift.
[06:22] Lena Schmidt: RoPE scaling - we've seen some models fail to extrapolate beyond training length. how do you approach large context extrapolation?
[06:30] Sofia Li: RoPE extrapolation is tricky. there are a few approaches: 1) linear scaling of rotary freq (xpos style), 2) Roformer/ALiBi-like biasing, 3) re-xl or chunked attention with local windows plus cross-window attention. for Llama variants we often use RoPE freq interpolation (rescale frequencies) to keep behavior stable up to 2x training length, but beyond that you get phase misalignment and model hallucination. we recommend staged tests: 8k -> 16k -> 32k with eval prompts.
[07:05] Priya Kapoor: is there any runtime trick to reduce memory for long RoPE contexts?
[07:10] Marcus Nguyen: windowed KV cache with summarized checkpoints: keep dense KV for last N tokens and compressed summaries for older history (vector sketching). it's lossy but reduces memory. also offload older KV pages to remote SSD with async prefetch for soon-to-be-used pages. performance depends on IO.
[07:30] Tomás Alvarez: on the offload: any recommended hardware? NVMe with PCIe4 is baseline, but will it still hit latency SLAs?
[07:38] Marcus Nguyen: for strict 200ms p50, offload will introduce jitter. NVMe over Fabric with RDMA helps, but then you're essentially designing a memory tier. Dedicated pools with large GPU memory or Multi-GPU with NVLink are simpler if you need deterministic tail latency.
[07:55] Jamie Park: let's talk through a concrete benchmark scenario for HelixAI: 70B Llama for chat, 1k tokens average, target p50 200ms, p95 < 700ms, mixed QPS peaking at 40 rps. what are the top tuning knobs?
[08:12] Sofia Li: list: 1) enable persistent prefix KV for same-user sessions; 2) partition router by prefix-hash so batching preserves cache locality; 3) set continuous batching window to 8-12ms; 4) evaluate Q4/gptq with calibration and guardrails; 5) for Dedicated use multi-GPU with NVLink and configure cross-GPU KV placement; 6) avoid MoE unless throughput-first batch serving.
[08:40] Priya Kapoor: calibration step - how invasive is it? do we need to fine-tune the model?
[08:45] Sofia Li: usually no full fine-tune. it's per-layer scale calibration or small adapter heads for logit rescaling. rarely we do a few-shot distillation pass on a tiny holdout set if quality drop is large. Redwood Optimize automates much of this pipeline.
[09:02] Tomás Alvarez: network and VPC questions - if we go Private with airgapped data plane, how does control plane reachability work?
[09:09] Marcus Nguyen: control plane can be optional; we support fully offline deploys where control plane is local. otherwise, control plane uses a small egress to Redwood for telemetry only and can be whitelisted. KM integration is customer-managed; we never store keys.
[09:25] Priya Kapoor: is there any SOC/ISO documentation you can share?
[09:28] Jamie Park: yes, we'll send SOC2 and ISO artifacts plus a security checklist and our onboarding runbook.
[09:34] Tomás Alvarez: back to MoE - any rule of thumb on where MoE wins cost-wise?
[09:40] Sofia Li: MoE wins when: 1) model capacity (parameters) matters and you have batchy throughput; 2) you can accept some latency variance; 3) you can afford engineering to integrate custom kernels. In practice, dense 2-4x quantization + sharded dense models often beat small MoE for latency-critical services.
[09:58] Lena Schmidt: what about costs on cloud GPUs vs dedicated metal - how to estimate routing overhead into cost?
[10:05] Marcus Nguyen: we model routing overhead as extra compute multiplier + memory fragmentation factor. e.g., for a MoE 8-expert model you might see a 1.4x effective compute on good infra, but on multi-tenant cloud GPUs it could be 1.8-2.2x due to scatter/gather inefficiencies and host side serialization. we provide a cost-estimator template; Sofia will attach the benchmark sheet.
[10:28] Priya Kapoor: any gotchas for Qwen family specifically?
[10:32] Sofia Li: Qwen has heavier rotary embedding per head and some custom positional handling; quantization recipes are less mature. also some Qwen checkpoints use fused kernels that don't map cleanly to gptq tooling, so expect more engineering time. but latency characteristics are nice for medium-sized models (6B-20B).
[10:50] Jamie Park: ok let's quick demo of a small benchmark we ran - Sofia you have slides?
[10:54] Sofia Li: yes i'll share screen (note: actual transcript doesn't include screen content). benchmark quick notes: Llama 70B dense vs Q4 gptq on p4d, continuous batching 10ms, batching by prefix-hash, result: p50 ~210ms when persistent KV enabled, p95 ~680ms. MoE variant (sparse routing) had p50 170ms but p95 spiked to 1.5s on same infra.
[11:22] Priya Kapoor: interesting the p50 improved but p95 worsened - that's consistent with routing jitter.
[11:28] Sofia Li: exactly - and memory overhead for MoE was 30% higher in that test due to expert replication.
[11:35] Tomás Alvarez: one more operational Q - how do you handle rollout and fallbacks if a new quantized variant degrades quality?
[11:42] Marcus Nguyen: we support canary rollouts per-route with automatic fallback to previous model version on quality/regression triggers. Redwood Optimize ties evaluations to prompt sets and can auto-roll back on metric drift.
[11:55] Priya Kapoor: any recommended A/B method for calibrating Q4 vs FP16 to measure hallucination increase?
[12:01] Sofia Li: use a stratified prompt set across instruction, long-context, and safety prompts. compute both automated metrics (perplexity, token-level confidence) and human eval samples. run at 1% traffic can give early warning without large user impact.
[12:18] Jamie Park: let's capture next steps - we'll run a focused benchmark for HelixAI with the recommended knobs. Marcus will prepare Dedicated config. Sofia will run calibration and attach the spreadsheet. Priya will share prompt sets and SLAs.
[12:35] Priya Kapoor: yep i'll share the prompt set and a few perf targets.
[12:40] Tomás Alvarez: we'll also gather infra network details and NVLink availability.
[12:44] Lena Schmidt: please include a section in the runbook about RoPE scaling tests and expected failure modes.
[12:49] Jamie Park: will do. ok last minute questions? (pause) cool thanks for the deep dive.
[12:58] -- End of recording --
